en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on the Indeterminate Rules (Aniyata-khaṇḍa)
2. The Second Training Rule on the Indeterminate At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī thought: “The Blessed One has prohibited [a monk] being alone with a woman...”
"to sit down alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed seat suitable for misconduct.
He sat down alone with that very maiden in a secluded place, conversing at appropriate times and speaking on the Dhamma at appropriate times.
A second time, Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, being invited, went to that family.
Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, saw the Venerable Udāyī sitting alone with that very young girl in private.
Seeing him, she said to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Venerable sir, this is not proper, it is not fitting, that the Master sits alone with a woman in private.”
"Venerable sir, although the noble one has no need for that teaching, nevertheless, people are difficult to convince and lack faith.
Even though the Venerable Udāyī was addressed thus by Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, he did not heed her.
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, went out and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the Venerable Udāyī sit alone with a woman in private?
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Is it true, Udāyī, that you sat alone with a woman in private?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How indeed, foolish man, could you sit alone with a woman in private?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Now, it may be that the seat is not concealed and not unsuitable for action, yet it is suitable for a woman to address with indecent words.
If a bhikkhu should sit down alone with a woman in such a seat, in private, and a trustworthy female lay follower,
having seen him, should charge him with one of two offenses— either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*— then [the bhikkhu] is guilty.”
“A monk who claims to be sitting [in private with a woman] is to be dealt with according to one of two rules: either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*.
Or he is to be dealt with according to whatever that trustworthy female lay follower says.
This rule, too, is undetermined.”
But it is not concealed; that is, it is not concealed by a wall, a door, a palm-leaf screen, a cloth curtain, a tree, a pillar, a granary, or by anything whatsoever—it is not concealed.
It is "not fit for use."
It is not possible to engage in sexual intercourse;
however, it is sufficient to address a woman with vulgar words,
for one is able to address a woman with vulgar words.
"But whoever" means whoever of such a kind... [as previously described] ...
"a bhikkhu."
...pe... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"In such a seat" means on a seat of this kind.

"Woman" means a human female, not a female spirit, not a female ghost, and not a female animal; one who is intelligent and capable of discerning what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken, and what is grave and what is trivial.
"Together with" means...
On one side:
"One comes alone" refers to both a monk and a woman.
"Secret" means a secret of the eye, a secret of the ear.
A secret of the eye means:
When the eye is being rubbed, or the eyebrow is being raised, or the head is being lifted, it is not possible to see;
as for the seclusion of the ear,
it is not possible to hear ordinary conversation.
“He may sit together” means:
when a woman is seated, the bhikkhu sits down near her or lies down near her;
or when the bhikkhu is seated, the woman sits down near him or lies down near him.
Both may be sitting, or both may be lying down. One whose word is trustworthy is called one who has realized the fruit,
who has attained direct knowledge, and who has understood the teaching.
A female lay follower (upāsikā) is one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
"Having seen" means:
Having seen [him], he should accuse him of one of two offenses: either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*.
When the monk admits to having sat down, he should be dealt with according to one of those two offenses: either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*.
Or rather, that bhikkhu should be dealt with according to what that trustworthy female lay follower says.
If she should say:
"I saw the venerable one sitting together with a woman, engaging in physical contact," [then he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits it, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If she should say,
"I saw the venerable one sitting together with a woman, engaging in physical contact," [he should be dealt with according to the offense].
If he should say,
“Truly I sat down, but I did not engage in physical contact,” he is to be dealt with for the act of sitting down …pe…
“I am not sitting, but rather lying down,” he should be made to lie down …pe… “I am not sitting,
but rather standing,” he should be made to stand.
He should not be made to do so.
But if she should say,
"I saw the venerable one lying down, engaging in physical contact with a woman," [then he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits that, he should be dealt with according to the offense...
[and so on] ... "It is true that I lay down, but I did not engage in physical contact," he should be dealt with for the act of lying down... [and so on].
“I am not lying down, but rather sitting,” he must be made to sit …pe… “I am not lying down,
but rather standing,” he must be made to stand.
He should not be made to do it.
If she should say,
"I heard from my noble master as he sat there addressing a woman with indecent words," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits that, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If she should say:
"I heard it from my noble sir while he was seated, as he was addressing a woman with vulgar words," [he should be dealt with according to the offense].
If he should say,
“It is true that I sat down, but I did not address him with offensive words,” he is to be dealt with for the act of sitting down. …pe…
“I am not sitting, but rather lying down,” he should be made to lie down …pe… “I am not sitting,
but rather standing,” he should be made to stand.
He should not be made to do it.
If she should say,
"I heard from my noble sir while he was lying down, as he was addressing a woman with vulgar words," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits that, he should be dealt with according to the offense... [etc.
... "I am indeed lying down, but I did not address him with wicked words," he should be dealt with for the act of lying down... [etc. ...
“I am not lying down, but rather sitting,” he should be made to sit …pe… “I am not lying down,
but rather standing,” he should be made to stand.
He must not be made to do so.
If she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one sitting alone with a woman in private," [he must not be made to do so].
If he admits it, he is to be dealt with for sitting down...
[and so on] ...if he says, "I was not sitting, but rather lying down," he is to be dealt with for lying down... [and so on].
“I am not sitting, but rather standing,” she should not be made to do it.
If she should say this:
“If the Venerable One was seen by me lying down alone with a woman in private,” and he admits it, he is to be dealt with for lying down;
… [or] “I did not lie down, but rather sat.”
He should be made to sit down … [and so on] … if he says,
"I am not lying down, but rather standing," he should not be made to do it.
This too is said with reference to the preceding [section].
It is "undetermined" (aniyata).
It is not fixed as either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*.
If one admits to going, admits to sitting, and admits to the offense, one is to be dealt with according to that offense.
If one admits to going, does not admit to sitting, but admits to the offense, one is to be dealt with according to that offense.
If he admits to going, admits to sitting, but does not admit to the offense, he should be dealt with for the sitting.
If he admits to going, does not admit to sitting, and does not admit to the offense, he should not be dealt with.
If he does not admit to going, admits to sitting, and admits to the offense, he should be dealt with for the offense.
If he does not acknowledge the going, does not acknowledge the sitting, but acknowledges the offense, he is to be dealt with according to the offense.
If he does not acknowledge the going, acknowledges the sitting, but does not acknowledge the offense, he is to be dealt with according to the sitting.
If he does not acknowledge the going, does not acknowledge the sitting, and does not acknowledge the offense, he is not to be dealt with.
The second undetermined offense is finished.
Venerable sirs, the two undetermined rules have been recited.
Regarding these, I ask the venerable ones: [Are you pure in this matter?]
“Are you pure in this matter?
A second time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter?”
A third time I ask:
"Are you pure in this matter?
The venerable ones are pure in this matter.
"Therefore, be silent;
thus do I hold this to be so. The summary verse for this is as follows:
It is both workable and likewise not [otherwise]; well-proclaimed,
it is indeterminate.
"By the Best of Buddhas, the Such-like One.
The Section on the Indeterminate is finished.
